## Purpose

Which vehicle classes have the highest average highway fuel economy, and how
much higher is highway mileage than city mileage in this dataset?

This vignette demonstrates how to use `dplyr` to select variables, filter rows,
create a variable, and summarize groups, then use `ggplot2` to visualize the
results. The example uses `ggplot2::mpg`, so no downloaded data file, API key,
or working-directory change is required.

## Setup and data source

Use R 4.1 or later for the native pipe, `|>`. If needed, run
`install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "knitr"))` once in the R console before
rendering. Package installation is deliberately kept outside the executable
analysis.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# mpg is included with ggplot2; copying it leaves the original data unchanged.
cars <- ggplot2::mpg
```

The [ggplot2 documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/mpg.html)
describes `mpg` as a subset of EPA fuel-economy data. It contains vehicle
configurations from 1999 and 2008. A model can appear in multiple rows because
its year, engine, transmission, or other characteristics can differ. A row
therefore represents a configuration, not a distinct model or a vehicle sale.

The main variables used here are `class` (vehicle class), `cty` (city miles per
gallon), and `hwy` (highway miles per gallon). Higher mpg means more distance
traveled per gallon of fuel.

## 1. Inspect and select the variables

`select()` chooses columns. `summarise()` without grouping produces one summary
row for the entire dataset. `n()` counts rows, while `n_distinct()` counts
different values.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-data
cars_selected <- cars |>
  select(manufacturer, model, year, class, cty, hwy)

data_check <- cars_selected |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    vehicle_classes = n_distinct(class),
    missing_class = sum(is.na(class)),
    missing_city = sum(is.na(cty)),
    missing_highway = sum(is.na(hwy))
  )

knitr::kable(data_check, caption = "Dataset size and missing-value checks")
```

## 2. Filter rows and create a new variable

`filter()` keeps rows satisfying the stated conditions. The checks below keep
records with a known class and positive, nonmissing mpg values. `mutate()` adds
`highway_gain`, the difference between highway and city mpg for each record.
For example, 30 highway mpg and 22 city mpg produce a gain of 8 mpg.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-data
cars_clean <- cars_selected |>
  filter(
    !is.na(class),
    !is.na(cty),
    !is.na(hwy),
    cty > 0,
    hwy > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(highway_gain = hwy - cty)

rows_removed <- nrow(cars_selected) - nrow(cars_clean)

knitr::kable(
  head(cars_clean, 6),
  caption = "First six records, including the new highway_gain variable"
)
```

The filters remove **`r rows_removed` records**, leaving **`r nrow(cars_clean)`**
for analysis. I retain both years and all vehicle configurations. I do not
remove repeated model names because configurations are legitimate observations.
No missing values are imputed, and mpg values are kept in their original units.

## 3. Group, summarize, and rank vehicle classes

`group_by(class)` makes the following calculations run separately for each
vehicle class. `summarise()` returns one row per class; `.groups = "drop"`
returns an ungrouped result. `arrange(desc(mean_highway))` sorts the class
averages from highest to lowest highway mpg.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-classes
class_summary <- cars_clean |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    mean_city = mean(cty),
    mean_highway = mean(hwy),
    mean_highway_gain = mean(highway_gain),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_highway))

# Round only the displayed table; keep full precision in class_summary.
knitr::kable(
  class_summary,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Class", "Records", "Mean city mpg", "Mean highway mpg",
                "Mean highway gain (mpg)"),
  caption = "Fuel economy by vehicle class, pooling 1999 and 2008"
)
```

## 4. Visualize the grouped results

`ggplot()` starts a plot and `aes()` maps variables to visual properties.
`geom_col()` uses the already calculated mean as the bar height. This differs
from the default `geom_bar()`, which counts rows. `reorder()` orders the class
labels by their highway averages, and `coord_flip()` makes the labels easier
to read.

```{r}
#| label: fig-highway-by-class
#| fig-cap: "Average highway mpg by vehicle class. Each configuration receives equal weight."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(class_summary, aes(x = reorder(class, mean_highway), y = mean_highway)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#356B8C", width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Compact cars have the highest average highway mpg in this sample",
    subtitle = "EPA configurations in ggplot2::mpg, 1999 and 2008 combined",
    x = "Vehicle class",
    y = "Mean highway fuel economy (mpg)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## Findings and limitations

```{r}
#| label: calculate-findings
# Take the first and last rows of the table already sorted by highway mpg.
highest_class <- class_summary |> slice_head(n = 1)
lowest_class <- class_summary |> slice_tail(n = 1)
overall_gain <- mean(cars_clean$highway_gain)
class_gap <- highest_class$mean_highway - lowest_class$mean_highway
```

- **`r highest_class$class`** has the highest class average highway fuel economy
  at **`r round(highest_class$mean_highway, 1)` mpg**, based on
  **`r highest_class$records` configurations**.
- **`r lowest_class$class`** has the lowest class average at
  **`r round(lowest_class$mean_highway, 1)` mpg**, based on
  **`r lowest_class$records` configurations**. The highest and lowest class
  averages differ by **`r round(class_gap, 1)` mpg**.
- Across all configurations, highway fuel economy exceeds city fuel economy
  by **`r round(overall_gain, 1)` mpg on average**. This is the average of the
  row-level differences, not an average of equally weighted class averages.

These are descriptive comparisons of this sample. The classes have different
numbers of configurations, and a class average can hide differences among its
models. Every configuration receives equal weight; these are not sales-weighted
averages. The data cover two historical years and a selected set of models, so
the findings should not be generalized to all cars or today's vehicle market.
The analysis does not establish that vehicle class causes a particular mpg.

This workflow shows how to move from row-level data to a readable comparison:
`select()` chooses variables, `filter()` checks usable records, `mutate()`
creates a measure, `group_by()` and `summarise()` calculate class statistics,
and `arrange()` and `ggplot2` make those results easier to interpret.

Save this file and click **Render** in RStudio, or run
`quarto render vignettes/akash_s_mpg.qmd` from the repository root. All results
are computed from the bundled dataset. The following records the R and package
versions used during rendering.
